questions.question: Which is a Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor?
questions.explanation: ESXi runs directly on hardware without a host OS underneath.

correct.explanation: VMware ESXi runs directly on bare metal — a Type 1 hypervisor.

incorrect.explanation: Workstation runs on top of Windows — Type 2 (hosted) hypervisor, not bare-metal Type 1.
incorrect.whatItDoes: VMware Workstation on Windows points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for ESXi runs directly on hardware without a host OS underneath.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "ESXi runs directly on hardware without a host OS underneath", VMware ESXi satisfies what this question tests — VMware Workstation on Windows does not.

incorrect.explanation: Docker Desktop is container tooling on a host OS — not a bare-metal hypervisor.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Docker Desktop only points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for ESXi runs directly on hardware without a host OS underneath.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "ESXi runs directly on hardware without a host OS underneath", VMware ESXi satisfies what this question tests — Docker Desktop only does not.

incorrect.explanation: A physical router forwards packets — it is not a hypervisor.
incorrect.whatItDoes: A physical router points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for ESXi runs directly on hardware without a host OS underneath.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "ESXi runs directly on hardware without a host OS underneath", VMware ESXi satisfies what this question tests — A physical router does not.

answerReview.examTip: Type 1 = bare metal (ESXi, Hyper-V on hardware). Type 2 = runs on OS (Workstation).

questions.question: A Type 2 hypervisor runs…
choices: On top of a host operating system
questions.explanation: Type 2 is hosted — e.g. Workstation on Windows/macOS.

correct.explanation: Type 2 (hosted) hypervisors install as an application on top of a host OS — e.g. VMware Workstation on Windows.

incorrect.explanation: Bare-metal-only describes Type 1 hypervisors (ESXi, Hyper-V on server) — Type 2 runs on a host operating system.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Directly on bare metal only points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Type 2 is hosted — e.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Type 2 is hosted — e", On top of a host operating system satisfies what this question tests — Directly on bare metal only does not.

incorrect.explanation: Containers are not hypervisors — Type 2 hypervisors run VMs as guest OS instances above the host OS.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Placing Type 2 hypervisor inside a container only
incorrect.whatItDoes: Inside a container only points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Type 2 is hosted — e.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Type 2 is hosted — e", On top of a host operating system satisfies what this question tests — Inside a container only does not.

incorrect.explanation: Type 2 hypervisors exist to run VMs — they require a host OS and create virtual machines on top of it.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Believing Type 2 hypervisors run without VMs
incorrect.whatItDoes: Without any VMs points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Type 2 is hosted — e.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Type 2 is hosted — e", On top of a host operating system satisfies what this question tests — Without any VMs does not.

answerReview.examTip: Type 1 = bare metal; Type 2 = hosted on a desktop/server OS.

questions.question: Containers differ from VMs because containers…
choices: Include a full guest OS each
questions.explanation: Containers isolate processes but share one kernel — lighter than full VMs.

correct.explanation: Containers share the host OS kernel — VMs each run a full guest OS.

incorrect.explanation: Full guest OS per instance describes VMs, not lightweight containers.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Include a full guest OS each points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for containers.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "containers", Share the host OS kernel satisfies what this question tests — Include a full guest OS each does not.

incorrect.explanation: Containers run extensively on Linux (Docker, containerd) — they don't require VMs.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Cannot run on Linux points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for containers.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "containers", Share the host OS kernel satisfies what this question tests — Cannot run on Linux does not.

incorrect.explanation: Containers virtualize workloads — they don't replace physical switches.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Replace physical switches points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for containers.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "containers", Share the host OS kernel satisfies what this question tests — Replace physical switches does not.

answerReview.examTip: VM = hypervisor + guest OS | Container = shared kernel + isolated processes.

questions.question: VRF on a router provides…
questions.explanation: VRF creates separate routing/forwarding instances on one device.

correct.explanation: VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding) creates multiple isolated routing/forwarding tables on one physical router.

incorrect.explanation: Wireless encryption (WPA/WPA2/WPA3) secures 802.11 frames — VRF segments Layer 3 routing instances.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Wireless encryption points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for VRF creates separate routing/forwarding instances on one device.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "VRF creates separate routing/forwarding instances on one device", Multiple isolated routing tables satisfies what this question tests — Wireless encryption does not.

incorrect.explanation: Fiber transceivers are physical Layer 1 optics — VRF is a control/data-plane virtualization feature.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Fiber transceiver support points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for VRF creates separate routing/forwarding instances on one device.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "VRF creates separate routing/forwarding instances on one device", Multiple isolated routing tables satisfies what this question tests — Fiber transceiver support does not.

incorrect.explanation: DHCP redundancy uses multiple servers or failover mechanisms — VRF isolates routing tables, not DHCP HA by itself.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: Expecting VRF to provide DHCP server redundancy
incorrect.whatItDoes: DHCP server redundancy points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for VRF creates separate routing/forwarding instances on one device.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "VRF creates separate routing/forwarding instances on one device", Multiple isolated routing tables satisfies what this question tests — DHCP server redundancy does not.

answerReview.examTip: VRF = separate routing tables on one router — like virtual routers sharing hardware.

questions.question: NFV (Network Function Virtualization) means…
choices: Running network services as software on general hardware
questions.explanation: NFV virtualizes functions like firewall and router as software.

correct.explanation: NFV runs network functions (firewall, router, load balancer) as software on commodity hardware instead of dedicated appliances.

incorrect.explanation: NFV virtualizes network services — it doesn't replace DNS with VLANs.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Replacing DNS with VLANs points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for NFV virtualizes functions like firewall and router as software.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "NFV virtualizes functions like firewall and router as software", Running network services as software on general hardware satisfies what this question tests — Replacing DNS with VLANs does not.

incorrect.explanation: NFV complements physical routing — it doesn't eliminate all routers.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Eliminating all routers points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for NFV virtualizes functions like firewall and router as software.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "NFV virtualizes functions like firewall and router as software", Running network services as software on general hardware satisfies what this question tests — Eliminating all routers does not.

incorrect.explanation: WEP is WLAN security — unrelated to Network Function Virtualization.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Using only WEP selects a weak or deprecated WLAN security option.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "NFV virtualizes functions like firewall and router as software", Running network services as software on general hardware satisfies what this question tests — Using only WEP does not.

answerReview.examTip: NFV = virtual firewall/router/LB on x86 | SDN = centralized control plane — often deployed together.

questions.question: Each virtual machine typically includes…
choices: Its own guest OS and virtual NICs
Shared kernel with all other VMs
questions.explanation: VMs are full guests with virtual hardware including vNICs.

correct.explanation: Each VM includes its own guest OS and virtual NICs — fully isolated from other VMs.

incorrect.explanation: A container image is lightweight — VMs bundle a full operating system.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: VM is only a container image
incorrect.whatItDoes: Only a container image points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for vm components.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "vm components", Its own guest OS and virtual NICs satisfies what this question tests — Only a container image does not.

incorrect.explanation: Shared kernel describes containers — each VM has its own kernel (guest OS).
incorrect.whatItDoes: Shared kernel with all other VMs points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for vm components.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "vm components", Its own guest OS and virtual NICs satisfies what this question tests — Shared kernel with all other VMs does not.

incorrect.explanation: VMs always have at least one vNIC for network connectivity.
incorrect.whatItDoes: No network interface points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for vm components.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "vm components", Its own guest OS and virtual NICs satisfies what this question tests — No network interface does not.

answerReview.examTip: Type 1 hypervisor (ESXi) vs Type 2 (Workstation) — both host VMs with guest OS + vNIC.

questions.question: True or False: VRF and VLAN provide the same type of isolation.
questions.explanation: False — VLAN = L2 broadcast domain; VRF = L3 routing table isolation.

correct.explanation: False — VRF isolates routing tables (Layer 3); VLAN isolates broadcast domains (Layer 2).

incorrect.explanation: True is wrong — VRF and VLAN solve different layers of isolation.
incorrect.misconceptionTested: VRF and VLAN same isolation type
incorrect.whatItDoes: True states the opposite of the tested fact about vrf vs vlan.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "vrf vs vlan", False satisfies what this question tests — True does not.

answerReview.examTip: VLAN = L2 broadcast domain | VRF = L3 routing instance — complementary, not interchangeable.

questions.question: Docker is commonly associated with…
questions.explanation: Docker packages apps into containers sharing the host kernel.

correct.explanation: Docker is the leading platform for container packaging and deployment.

incorrect.explanation: Type 1 hypervisors (ESXi, Hyper-V) run VMs — Docker runs containers.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Type 1 hypervisors points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Docker packages apps into containers sharing the host kernel.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Docker packages apps into containers sharing the host kernel", Container packaging and deployment satisfies what this question tests — Type 1 hypervisors does not.

incorrect.explanation: WPA3 is wireless security — Docker is container orchestration.
incorrect.whatItDoes: WPA3 points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Docker packages apps into containers sharing the host kernel.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Docker packages apps into containers sharing the host kernel", Container packaging and deployment satisfies what this question tests — WPA3 does not.

incorrect.explanation: Spanning Tree prevents L2 loops — Docker is application containerization.
incorrect.whatItDoes: Spanning Tree points to a related idea, but not the specific behavior or value required for Docker packages apps into containers sharing the host kernel.
incorrect.whyWrongHere: For "Docker packages apps into containers sharing the host kernel", Container packaging and deployment satisfies what this question tests — Spanning Tree does not.

answerReview.examTip: Docker/Kubernetes = containers | VMware/Hyper-V = VMs — different virtualization models.
